y-m-78-12.title: How set mean and standard deviation so about 5% defects?
y-m-78-12.topic: Design specification using roughly 95% interval of normal distribution
y-m-78-12.goal: Use rule about 95% within 2 SD around mean to interpret production mean/SD conditions; choose among settings and state risk.
y-m-78-12.material: Snack factory bag weight (g) assumed normal with mean μ and standard deviation σ. Spec 95g to 107g; outside defective. Using rule about 95% within μ−2σ to μ+2σ, for defects around 5% or less we require this interval inside spec. ±2 standard deviations.
y-m-78-12.thinking.0: Turn rule into conditions and find multiple solutions
y-m-78-12.thinking.1: Check if a setting meets conditions
y-m-78-12.thinking.2: Say how to check normal-distribution assumption
y-m-78-12.prereq.1: Approximate normal curve shape (center at mean, symmetric)
y-m-78-12.prereq.2: Rule of thumb: around 95% data within 2 standard deviations of mean
y-m-78-12.s.s1.prompt: Choose all three process settings meeting 'defects about 5% or less'. (A: mean 101g, SD 3g; B: mean 100g, SD 2g; C: mean 104g, SD 2g)
y-m-78-12.s.s1.hint.0: For each setting find μ−2σ and μ+2σ, compare with 95 to 107g specification.
y-m-78-12.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether interval fall below lower limit or above upper.
y-m-78-12.s.s1.r.a: A interval 95 to 107g; B interval 96 to 104g. Both inside specification.
y-m-78-12.s.s1.r.b: B interval (mean ±2σ) is 96 to 104g, inside spec too.
y-m-78-12.s.s1.r.c: C interval 100 to 108g, so 108 exceed upper limit 107; more defects on that side.
y-m-78-12.s.s1.r.d: C interval 100 to 108g, exceeding upper limit.
y-m-78-12.s.s1.r.e: C mean high, so interval exceed 107g upper spec.
y-m-78-12.s.s1.explain: A interval 95 to 107g and B 96 to 104g, both within spec. C 100 to 108g, 1g above 107 upper limit, so defect rate may pass 5%.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.prompt:
Find 3 different process settings (mean μ, SD σ) meeting factory requirements.
① μ−2σ≥95 and μ+2σ≤107 (defects around 5% or less)
② Mean at least labelled weight 100g (μ≥100)
③ SD at least 1g (σ≥1, because finer control costs much)
y-m-78-12.s.s2.hint.0: Choose mean first; find distances from mean to lower/upper spec edges.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.hint.1: Think how shorter distance limits maximum SD.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.ok.c1: Interval of two standard deviations around mean lies inside specification. 2 SD.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.fail.c1: Interval μ−2σ to μ+2σ goes outside specification 95 to 107g.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.fail.c3: Standard deviation must be at least 1g.
y-m-78-12.s.s2.explain: Many settings meet conditions. Examples: (100,2) gives 96–104g; (101,2.5) gives 96–106g; (102,2) gives 98–106g. Mean closer to spec middle (101g) lets SD be larger. Settings (100,2), (101,2.5), (102,2). Values: 100, 2; 101, 2.5; 102, 2.
y-m-78-12.s.s3.prompt: Choose one setting you made (write numbers) and tell factory manager in 2 or 3 sentences 'use it, but what must we check'. Include assumptions and how to check them.
y-m-78-12.s.s3.hint.0: First calculate and write your chosen setting interval μ−2σ to μ+2σ.
y-m-78-12.s.s3.hint.1: Imagine if data no normal (e.g. skewed one side).
y-m-78-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You show numbers proving chosen setting meets all ① to ③?
y-m-78-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You specify how check normality (weigh bags, histogram, etc.)?
y-m-78-12.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You mention if assumption wrong, defect rate change?
y-m-78-12.s.s3.model.0: With mean 100g and SD 2g, about 95% fall in 96–104g, inside spec. But this assumes bag weights normal (bell curve); weigh a few hundred bags and check histogram symmetry.
y-m-78-12.s.s3.model.1: Mean 102g and SD 2g gives 98–106g, within 95–107g. This assumes weights spread symmetrically around mean, so regularly check actual measurements' distribution, mean and SD; adjust setting if wrong.

y-m-78-08.title: What does correlation coefficient −0.6 tell us, and what doesn't it tell us?
y-m-78-08.topic: Meaning and limits of correlation coefficient
y-m-78-08.goal: Know coefficient shows direction/strength of straight-line relationship, not slope or cause. Make example where coefficient near 0 but relationship clear.
y-m-78-08.material: Correlation between smartphone-use hours and sleep hours for 20 students is −0.6. Scatter plot points form generally downward band. Coefficient from −1 to 1 shows direction and strength of linear relationship (0 means no linear relationship visible).
y-m-78-08.thinking.0: Finding errors in statements interpreting correlation
y-m-78-08.prereq.0: H2 here means one step beyond H1 in production difficulty only; no grade assignment. Assume prerequisites below.
y-m-78-08.prereq.1: Reading positive/negative relation of two variables from scatterplot
y-m-78-08.prereq.2: Correlation coefficient between −1 and 1 showing linear relationship strength
y-m-78-08.prereq.3: Reading table and substituting into formula
y-m-78-08.s.s1.prompt: Student interprets coefficient −0.6. Choose one wrong line.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.hint.0: Classify each line: direction, strength, slope, or cause.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine line 5 applied to scatterplot with U-shaped points.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.line.0: Longer use tends to go with shorter sleep.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.line.1: So each 1-hour increase in use reduces sleep by 0.6 hours.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.line.2: How far relationship departs from straight line is shown by coefficient size.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.line.3: From this data alone, hard to say for sure smartphone caused sleep reduction.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.line.4: If coefficient 0, there'd be no relationship at all between variables.
y-m-78-08.s.s1.explain: Lines 2 and 5 are wrong. Line 2: coefficient shows direction and strength, not slope; change in hours per 1-hour increase needs separate regression line. Line 5: coefficient 0 means no linear relationship; curved relationships can still exist.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.prompt: Choose all scatter plots where coefficient near 0 but variables clearly related (plots described in words).
y-m-78-08.s.s2.hint.0: For each shape, see if y overall moves one direction as x grows.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.hint.1: Split x into left and right halves and compare trends.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.o.a: Points form straight band lower-left to upper-right.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.r.a: Near-straight band has correlation coefficient absolute value near 1.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.r.b: For left-right symmetric curve, trends in opposite directions cancel; coefficient can be near 0.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.r.c: Coefficient near 0 because no relationship, but this isn't a clear relationship case.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.r.d: In ring, for fixed x, y splits into two values, so coefficient may be near 0.
y-m-78-08.s.s2.explain: Coefficient measures linear relations only. A clear nonlinear rule like U shape can have relation while coefficient near 0. Random scatter (c) has no relation.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.prompt:
Let x be −2, −1, 0, 1, 2; choose y by a rule. For 5 points, give 2 examples where correlation is 0 and x clearly determines y. (y1...y5 are y values for x=−2,−1,0,1,2; integers.)
① y symmetric about x=0 (y1=y5, y2=y4)
② y1,y2,y3 keep increasing or decreasing (U or ∩ shape). −2 −1 0 1 2 5 2 0 −2 −1 0 1 2 0 3 4
y-m-78-08.s.s3.hint.0: Check sum of products when y at x=−2 equals y at x=2.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.hint.1: Choose values one by one so y1,y2,y3 keep decreasing (e.g. large to small).
y-m-78-08.s.s3.fail.c1: Not true that y1=y5 and y2=y4.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.ok.c2: y1,y2,y3 keep increasing or keep decreasing.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.fail.c2: y1,y2,y3 don't move in one direction only.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.ok.c4: Sum of x·y products is 0, so correlation coefficient is 0.
y-m-78-08.s.s3.explain: Mean x is 0, so if sum x·y is 0, correlation is 0. Symmetric points give product sum 0. Example y=x² gives (4,1,0,1,4), x fully determines y but correlation is 0. 0 0 0 0 4 1 0 1 4 0

y-m-78-11.thinking.2: Make several cases wey meet conditions
y-m-78-11.prereq.0: H2 here means one step beyond H1 in production difficulty only; no grade assignment. Assume prerequisites below.
y-m-78-11.title: They say test 90% accurate, so if I test positive, am I 90% likely infected?
y-m-78-11.topic: Meaning of positive result and prevalence (practical conditional probability)
y-m-78-11.goal: Know chance positive result means real infection depend on test performance and share infected too; create several cases meeting conditions.
y-m-78-11.material: Test for infectious disease come positive for '90 out of 100 infected people' (sensitivity 90%). Minsu test positive. He think, 'Test 90% accurate, so chance say I infected na 90%.' We never know how many infected people dey in test group, and how many positives among uninfected.
y-m-78-11.thinking.0: Sort information we need for judgment
y-m-78-11.thinking.1: Reason with concrete number like 1,000 people 1000 people.
y-m-78-11.prereq.1: Set whole group as number (e.g. 1000) and count each subgroup
y-m-78-11.prereq.3: Meaning of sensitivity (positive share among infected) and specificity (negative share among uninfected)
y-m-78-11.s.s1.prompt: To check Minsu judgment 'chance I infected na 90%', what more information needed? Choose all.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.hint.0: Write two kinds of people among positive results separately.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.hint.1: Think what you need know to find each group's size.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.o.a: Count of people who pay test fee
y-m-78-11.s.s1.r.a: Fee no connect to meaning of result.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.o.b: Proportion truly infected among people taking test
y-m-78-11.s.s1.r.b: Same positive result mean different thing when infected rare versus common.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.r.d: How often positive comes even when no infection change meaning of positive.
y-m-78-11.s.s1.explain: Positive people mix 'positive among infected' and 'positive among uninfected'. Need sizes of both groups (infected share) and positive share among uninfected to know true-infection share among positives.
y-m-78-11.s.s2.prompt:
Sensitivity 90%, 1000 people tested. Infected count p; share negative among uninfected (specificity) k%. Choose p and k so at least half positive people truly infected (infected positives ≥ uninfected positives); enter 3 combinations.
① p integer 1 to 500
② k integer 90 to 99
③ Infected positives (0.9×p) no less than uninfected positives ((100−k)%×(1000−p))
y-m-78-11.s.s2.hint.0: Choose p; find infected positives and uninfected total, then change k and see how uninfected positive count move.
y-m-78-11.s.s2.hint.1: Check if you can raise p when k low and lower p when k high.
y-m-78-11.s.s2.ok.c3: At least half positive results are infected.
y-m-78-11.s.s2.fail.c3: Among positives, infected are under half. Need 90×p ≥ (100−k)×(1000−p).
y-m-78-11.s.s2.explain: If p=20,k=99, of 20 infected people 18 positive; of 980 uninfected people, 1% or 9.8 positive. So at least half (about 65%) positives infected. Same test can do this only where infected common (p high) or specificity high.
y-m-78-11.s.s3.prompt: Think about p=20,k=95 (20 infected among 1000; specificity 95%). In 1 or 2 sentences explain to Minsu why positive result may still mean infection chance far below 90%.
y-m-78-11.s.s3.hint.0: Split 1000 people into infected and uninfected, write count positive in each.
y-m-78-11.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many positive people are infected.
y-m-78-11.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Infected people na ... while uninfected ...
y-m-78-11.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You compare uninfected positives (around 49) with infected positives (18)?
y-m-78-11.s.s3.selfAssess.1: You say which kind most positive results come from?
y-m-78-11.s.s3.selfAssess.2: You explain not as 'test bad' but 'group makeup changes probability'?
y-m-78-11.s.s3.model.0: Only 20 of 1000 infected, so 90% of them (18) test positive. But 5% of 980 uninfected, about 49, also positive. Of about 67 positives, only 18 infected, so chance about 27%.
y-m-78-11.s.s3.model.1: Not because test wrong, but because uninfected people far more numerous. Even 5% of healthy 980 gives around 49 false positives, more than 18 infected positives; so positive result still low chance of infection.
y-m-78-11.s.s3.modelNote.1: This answer explain by comparing counts.

y-m-78-01.title: Two box plots: can we say A faster?
y-m-78-01.topic: Comparing groups with box plots: overlap and what can be read
y-m-78-01.goal: Separate what box plot can/can't show for sure; consider small median difference, box overlap, and data count when judging confidence.
y-m-78-01.material:
Two local snack shops A and B published delivery times from order to arrival (minutes) of recent orders as box plots. Here are the values.

| | Minimum | First quartile | Median | Third quartile | Maximum |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 15 | 23 | 28 | 38 | 55 |
| B | 20 | 26 | 31 | 40 | 52 |

First quartile is where lower quarter ends; third quartile is where upper quarter starts. Box covers values between Q1 and Q3: middle half. Shorter delivery is better. App manager wants label A 'faster shop'.
y-m-78-01.thinking.0: Comparing median difference and box length (spread) together
y-m-78-01.thinking.1: Sorting what box plot alone can and can't tell
y-m-78-01.thinking.2: Rechecking judgment/confidence after learning data count
y-m-78-01.prereq.0: This platform's production label H1 means introductory high-school difficulty; doesn't assign subject to particular grade. Assume prerequisite ideas below.
y-m-78-01.prereq.1: Reading minimum, first quartile, median, third quartile and maximum from box plot
y-m-78-01.prereq.2: Median is middle value after sorting data by size
y-m-78-01.s.s1.prompt: From box plots alone, first judge whether manager can label A faster. What is best judgment?
y-m-78-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write numbers for range where boxes overlap.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.hint.1: Find median difference (minutes) and box lengths (minutes), compare.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.o.a: A median lower, so every A order arrives faster than every B order.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.r.a: Median is one middle value, not comparison of every value. A max 55 greater than B max 52.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.o.b: Medians differ 3 min and boxes overlap a lot, so clear difference hard to claim.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.r.b: You consider small median gap and middle-half overlap together. There is a tendency one way, but careful about size.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.o.c: Boxes similar length, so shops' delivery times exactly same.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.r.c: Box lengths about 15 and 14 minutes are similar, but medians differ by 3. 'Exactly same' too strong.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.o.d: B fastest order 20 min, slower than A fastest 15, so every B order slower than every A order.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.r.d: One minimum can't compare every order. A middle half (box) is 23–38 min, so many A orders took longer than B minimum 20.
y-m-78-01.s.s1.explain: Boxes overlap greatly around 26–38 min. A median 3 min smaller hints A tends slightly faster; doesn't mean all or most A deliveries faster.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.prompt: Choose all things knowable from box plot alone.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.hint.0: Find which of five box-plot values each choice comes from.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.hint.1: Check if options mix in things not shown by those values (counts, weather, etc.).
y-m-78-01.s.s2.o.a: At A, at least half orders arrived within 28 minutes.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.r.a: You use median meaning: at least half values at or below median.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.o.b: At B, more than half orders arrived within 30 minutes.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.r.b: B median 31 means at least half took 31 min or more. So 30 or less can't be more than half.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.r.c: Box plot doesn't show data count; must state separately.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.o.d: At B, about a quarter orders took 40 minutes or more.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.r.d: You use third quartile meaning; upper quarter is at or above it.
y-m-78-01.s.s2.explain: Median means at least half at/below value; third quartile means about quarter at/above. Counts and specific time/weather info aren't in box plot.
y-m-78-01.s.s3.prompt: New info: each plot used only 'latest 20 orders'. Is your initial judgment unchanged? Explain and name at least one data type that would strengthen it.
y-m-78-01.s.s3.hint.0: Put first judgment and new fact side by side.
y-m-78-01.s.s3.hint.1: In one sentence say how 20 data points affect belief in 3-minute difference.
y-m-78-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: My first judgment was ... because ...
y-m-78-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you link initial judgment to new fact, explaining why keep/change it?
y-m-78-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you include reasons both for A faster and for caution?
y-m-78-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Would extra data requested really help (e.g. more orders, time-of-day breakdown)?
y-m-78-01.s.s3.model.0: I keep my first judgment. Medians A=28, B=31, only 3 min apart; boxes overlap a lot. With only 20 orders, chance may explain gap, so can't be sure A faster. I'd gather more orders and check.
y-m-78-01.s.s3.model.1: I soften my judgment. Medians suggest A tends faster, but 20 orders is small, so confidence falls. Need at least latest 100 orders per shop and time-of-day data like lunch/dinner.
y-m-78-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: Keeping or revising both valid if reason given.
y-m-78-01.s.s3.model.2: My first judgment weakens. With 20 cases, 3-minute median gap may be chance. I'd like several months of order data.

y-m-78-02.prereq.0: This platform's production label H1 means introductory high-school difficulty; doesn't assign subject to particular grade. Assume prerequisite ideas below.
y-m-78-02.title: If weights change, does ranking change?
y-m-78-02.topic: Weighted average: converted scores vary with weights
y-m-78-02.goal: Confirm two students' converted-score order can change with weights, find several weights meeting conditions, discuss fairness of choosing weights.
y-m-78-02.material:
Semester grade combines written test and performance scores using weights to produce score out of 100. Written weight p%, performance q%, p+q=100. Both tests out of 100.

| | Written | Performance |
|---|---|---|
| Minseo | 72 | 96 |
| Doyun | 94 | 70 |

Assume scores fixed; weights not yet decided.
y-m-78-02.thinking.0: Finding several values meeting multiple conditions
y-m-78-02.thinking.1: Examining weighting effect on each student separately
y-m-78-02.thinking.2: Discussing why criteria must be set beforehand
y-m-78-02.prereq.2: A course grade combines assessment scores using set weights.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.prompt: If written weight rises (e.g. 40% to 60%), how expect scores change for both students?
y-m-78-02.s.s1.hint.0: For p=40 and p=60, calculate both converted scores and place side by side.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.hint.1: See direction each score moves as p grows.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.o.a: Whatever written weight is, students' ranking always same.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.r.a: For rank to always stay same, one student would need higher scores on both tests. Here each has strength in a different test.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.o.b: If written weight increases, both scores go up.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.r.b: Weighting doesn't create points; it changes which score counts more. Student with lower score in one part may drop.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.o.c: Minseo has bigger gap between her scores, so her converted score always higher regardless of weights.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.r.c: Big gap doesn't guarantee high converted score. Which score receives more weight matters.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.o.d: If written weight rises, Doyun gains and Minseo loses.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.r.d: You state direction: student with higher written score gains, lower loses. Calculation can find percent where rank switches.
y-m-78-02.s.s1.explain: As p grows, Doyun (94), with higher written mark, gains; Minseo (96), with stronger performance mark, loses. They tie at p≈54.2% (72p+96q=94p+70q, p+q=100).
y-m-78-02.s.s2.prompt:
Enter 2 different weight pairs meeting these conditions (written p%, performance q%; both integers):
① p+q=100
② Both written and performance weights at least 20%
③ Minseo converted score at least 85
④ Doyun converted score at least 80
y-m-78-02.s.s2.hint.0: First roughly find p range meeting only ③, then range meeting only ④, and see overlap.
y-m-78-02.s.s2.hint.1: Choose p, calculate both converted scores, change p by 1 and compare movements.
y-m-78-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Each weight must be integer at least 20.
y-m-78-02.s.s2.fail.c3: Minseo score below 85. (72×p+96×q must be at least 8500)
y-m-78-02.s.s2.fail.c4: Doyun score below 80. (94×p+70×q must be at least 8000)
y-m-78-02.s.s2.explain: Only integer weight pairs satisfying conditions are written 42%–45%. At 41%, Doyun below 80; at 46%, Minseo below 85. Initially possible range narrows because effects go opposite directions.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.prompt: Judge if school may set weights by 'adjusting them after seeing two students' scores'.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.hint.0: Check where scores were used in conditions ①–④.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.hint.1: To call criterion fair, consider how to explain when it is set and who it applies to.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.o.a: Choose weights after scores come out to raise preferred student's mark.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.r.a: If criteria chosen after seeing results, they target a particular student.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.o.b: Set weights before test and use equally for all students.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.r.b: You note criteria set before scores and applied same to everyone.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.o.c: For each student separately, use weighting that gives that student highest score.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.r.c: If criteria differ by student, their converted scores can't be compared fairly.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.o.d: Weights don't affect converted scores, so any choice fine.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.r.d: As you calculated, converted scores and ranking change depending on weighting.
y-m-78-02.s.s3.explain: You confirmed weights change scores and ranking. Set them before results, aligned with assessment purpose, and apply equally. Here finding weights meeting conditions was practice to understand their effect.

y-m-78-03.prereq.0: This platform's production label H1 means introductory high-school difficulty; doesn't assign subject to particular grade. Assume prerequisite ideas below.
y-m-78-03.title: A 12-point gap and an 18-point gap: which is bigger?
y-m-78-03.topic: Comparing scores on different tests using standard deviation
y-m-78-03.goal: Compare test scores using distance from mean and spread (standard deviation); state assumptions needed for trustworthy comparison.
y-m-78-03.material:
Hayun scored 82 Korean and 74 math in same grade. Grade results (tests out of 100):

| | Hayun score | Grade mean | Standard deviation (score spread around mean) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Korean | 82 | 70 | 6 |
| Math | 74 | 56 | 12 |

Hayun says, 'In math I'm 18 above mean and Korean 12 above, so I did better in math.'
y-m-78-03.thinking.0: Comparing values on different scales against same standard
y-m-78-03.thinking.1: Finding line where comparison standard misused
y-m-78-03.thinking.2: Stating conditions under which comparison holds
y-m-78-03.prereq.1: Meaning of mean and standard deviation (spread around mean)
y-m-78-03.s.s1.prompt: Hayun says, 'I'm 18 points above mean in math, so math is where I did relatively better.' What is best judgment about position within grade?
y-m-78-03.s.s1.hint.0: For each subject, find how many standard deviations score is above mean; compare.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think how spread around mean changes meaning of 12 vs 18 points.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.o.a: Korean (82), with higher actual score, is where she did relatively better.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.r.a: Meaning of high score depends whether test easy or hard. Compare with grade mean.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.o.b: Math, with larger gap from mean (18), is better.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.r.b: You compare raw gaps. Math scores are more spread out, so 18 means something different from Korean's 12.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.o.c: Using standard deviation as unit, compare how many SDs from mean: Korean position higher.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.r.c: You switch to distance scaled by data spread, making score units comparable.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.o.d: We don't know test difficulty or distribution shape, so can't judge position.
y-m-78-03.s.s1.r.d: Careful to want distribution shape, but with mean and SD given, first see if comparison possible using them.

y-m-78-04.material:
Survey record average daily sleep (hours) for 30 students at one school (recorded in 0.5-hour steps). Same data shown in three tables with different intervals. 'At least ~ less than' means include first value, exclude last.

**Table A (start at 5 hours, width 1 hour)**
| Class (hours) | 5~6 | 6~7 | 7~8 | 8~9 | 9~10 | 10~11 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Student count | 3 | 7 | 13 | 5 | 1 | 1 |

**Table B (start at 5.5 hours, width 1 hour)**
| Class (hours) | 5.5~6.5 | 6.5~7.5 | 7.5~8.5 | 8.5~9.5 | 9.5~10.5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Student count | 7 | 12 | 8 | 2 | 1 |

**Table C (start at 4 hours, width 2 hours)**
| Class (hours) | 4~6 | 6~8 | 8~10 | 10~12 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Student count | 3 | 20 | 6 | 1 |

y-m-78-05.title: Daily sales fell: is the business going downhill?
y-m-78-05.topic: Read time series with weekday patterns: compare same weekdays and 7-day averages
y-m-78-05.goal: For repeating-pattern data, don't decide trend from one-day gap alone. Compare same weekdays or 7-day averages and judge how new info changes possible cause.
y-m-78-05.material: Neighbourhood bakery owner record daily sales by weekday. This Sunday sales lower than last Saturday; owner worried. Values recorded same time daily at this bakery; only similar-scale days included (no public holidays).
y-m-78-05.thinking.0: Update judgment and confidence as data grow

y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Week 2 Friday (150) pass Monday (108), so sales growing.

y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: All seven days fall, but only two weeks; no know whether continue. 7 days.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You point out fact of decrease and whether it continues na separate.
y-m-78-05.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Total fell, so bakery definitely in steady decline.

y-m-78-06.material:

y-m-78-06.s.s2.explain: Example: A rises 100 to 115, +15 points (15%); B rises 160 to 180, +20 points (12.5%). A's point increase smaller, but growth rate higher. Same point change looks larger as ratio when base index small. 100 115 15 15 160 180 20 12.5 2021
y-m-78-06.s.s3.prompt: Student says, 'A 2023 index 130 and B 110, so A costs more than B.' What judgment fits?

y-m-78-06.s.s3.r.a: Each index uses its own item's base-year price as 100. It doesn't directly compare prices of different items.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.o.b: Index compares each item with its own base year, so actual price unknown.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.o.c: A's point change is always bigger than B's in 2023.

y-m-78-06.s.s3.r.d: Index difference isn't price difference; units differ.
y-m-78-06.s.s3.explain: Index means 'base-year price set to 100', useful for comparing one item's change over time. To compare different items or actual prices, need base-year prices.

y-m-78-10.title: 52% support, margin ±3.1%p: can we say it's a majority?
y-m-78-10.topic: Reading confidence interval: can we say majority?
y-m-78-10.goal: Judge strength by whether interval includes reference 50%; explain how larger sample changes judgment and what 95% means.
y-m-78-10.material: City surveys support/opposition to new library. Of 1,000 randomly selected residents, 52% support; 95% confidence interval about 48.9%–55.1% (margin ±3.1%p). Reporter wants headline 'Majority support'. Survey by phone; assume response rate not low.
y-m-78-10.thinking.0: Judging by comparing confidence interval with reference value
y-m-78-10.thinking.1: Evaluating how new data affects judgment
y-m-78-10.prereq.1: Sample proportion vs population proportion, and why samples vary
y-m-78-10.prereq.2: Reading ± margin of error as interval endpoints
y-m-78-10.prereq.3: Rough idea what 95% confidence interval represents
y-m-78-10.s.s1.prompt: What is best judgment about headline 'Majority support'?
y-m-78-10.s.s1.hint.0: Compare interval's lower and upper ends with 50%.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.hint.1: Think one reason sample proportion may differ from all residents' proportion.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.o.a: Sample result 52% exceeds 50%, so okay to call majority.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.r.a: You treat sample proportion 52% as population proportion. It can vary across surveys.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.o.b: Margin of error means survey inaccurate, so meaningless.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.r.b: Interval 48.9–55.1 carries information: support isn't very low or very high.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.o.c: Interval includes 50%; this survey alone can't say for sure it's a majority.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.r.c: You judge conclusion strength by whether interval includes reference 50%.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.o.d: If value is in confidence interval, it's equally likely at edge or center.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.r.d: Values nearer interval center tend to be more likely; edges aren't equal.
y-m-78-10.s.s1.explain: 95% interval 48.9–55.1 means we can't rule out population support below 50%. Hard to claim 'majority' from this survey alone.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.prompt: New info: when sample increased to 4,000 using same method, survey again show 51.6% support, 95% confidence interval about 50.1% to 53.1% (margin error ±1.5%p). Now what judgment fit best?
y-m-78-10.s.s2.hint.0: Put both intervals side by side and compare width (upper minus lower).
y-m-78-10.s.s2.hint.1: Use numbers check how near lower bound to 50%.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.o.a: Confidence interval above 50%, so at 95% level we fit say majority.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.r.a: You compare interval with reference number. Na statistical reading.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.o.b: Lower bound very close to 50%, so slim majority; other factors matter too.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.r.b: You add caution to statistical judgment.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.o.c: First survey (52%) and second (51.6%) differ, so neither trustworthy.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.r.c: Small difference between surveys natural. Confidence interval reflect this kind fluctuation.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.o.d: Sample four times bigger, so survey no error at all now. 4 times.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.r.d: Bigger sample reduce error but no remove am. Margin ±1.5%p remain.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.explain: Sample bigger and interval narrower; lower bound 50.1%, just above 50. At 95% level call majority, but margin slim, so consider survey method and other factors.
y-m-78-10.s.s2.acc.0: 95% interval above 50%, so statistically valid to call majority at 95% level. But mention difference slim and factors beyond sampling error still matter.

y-m-78-13.title: Finishers lost 3.2 kg on average: was it challenge effect?
y-m-78-13.topic: Survivorship bias and rewriting an ad claim
y-m-78-13.goal: Know excluding dropouts can inflate effect; create example where completer average differs greatly from overall average; rewrite ad so reader not misled.
y-m-78-13.material: Exercise app advertise: 'Average weight loss of 30-day challenge finishers: 3.2 kg!' People join voluntarily; app keeps no record of people quitting midway.
y-m-78-13.thinking.0: Sort info needed to judge effect
y-m-78-13.thinking.1: Create example where overall average lower than subgroup average
y-m-78-13.prereq.1: Find overall mean from group means and group sizes
y-m-78-13.s.s1.prompt: To judge challenge effect from phrase alone, what more info needed? Choose all.
y-m-78-13.s.s1.hint.0: First state which people the phrase averages over.
y-m-78-13.s.s1.hint.1: Think who left out and whether their results raise or lower average.
y-m-78-13.s.s1.o.a: Number who started and proportion who finished
y-m-78-13.s.s1.r.a: Same average mean different things depending on what share of starters finished.
y-m-78-13.s.s1.o.b: Total app downloads and number who saw ad
y-m-78-13.s.s1.r.b: Download count no directly connect to challenge result.
y-m-78-13.s.s1.o.c: Weight changes recorded for people who quit
y-m-78-13.s.s1.r.c: Leaving dropouts out makes average only for people with good results.
y-m-78-13.s.s1.o.d: Ad model age, filming place and date
y-m-78-13.s.s1.r.d: Model age and filming location no connect to challenge effect.
y-m-78-13.s.s1.o.e: Weight changes of similar people who did not join
y-m-78-13.s.s1.r.e: Without comparison, no know whether 3.2kg due to challenge.
y-m-78-13.s.s1.explain: Need starter completion share, dropout results, and comparison with nonparticipants. Downloads or model age irrelevant to effect.
y-m-78-13.s.s2.prompt:
Suppose 200 people started; finishers (f people) lost average 3.2kg, dropouts (200−f people) lost g kg (negative means gained). Enter 2 different (f,g) making overall loss average at most 1kg.
① f integer 10 to 190
② g from −1 to 1
③ Overall average (3.2×f+g×(200−f))÷200 ≤1 200 starters.
y-m-78-13.s.s2.hint.0: Use some values check how overall average move if finisher count small.
y-m-78-13.s.s2.hint.1: Change dropout average g; calculate left side of condition ③ and compare with 1.
y-m-78-13.s.s2.fail.c1: Finisher count f must be integer 10 to 190.
y-m-78-13.s.s2.fail.c2: Dropout average loss g must be from −1 to 1 kg.
y-m-78-13.s.s2.ok.c3: Overall average is 1 kg or less.
y-m-78-13.s.s2.explain: For example, if 50 of 200 finish and 150 dropouts average 0.2 kg, whole-group average is (160+30)÷200=0.95 kg. Finisher-only average 3.2 kg is correct, but average of everyone who started may be much lower.
